prompt: What is a polymer?

choices.text: A large molecule built by joining many smaller molecules, called monomers
A small molecule that joins with many others to build a large one
choices.why: That describes a monomer, the building block.

choices.text: A mixture of many different small molecules that are not bonded together
choices.why: A polymer is a single large molecule made of repeating units joined by bonds.

choices.text: Any small molecule that contains a carbon–carbon double bond
choices.why: That describes an alkene, which may serve as a monomer. The polymer is the large molecule made from many monomers.

explanation: A polymer is a large, sometimes very large, molecule built up by repetitive joining of many smaller molecules called monomers. Polyethylene, for example, is made from ethylene monomers.

prompt: Which pairing of a biological polymer with its monomer is correct?

choices.why: Proteins are built from amino acids; nucleic acids are built from nucleotides.
Nucleic acids are built from nucleotides.
Cellulose is built of repeating glucose units.

explanation: Cellulose is a polymer of repeating glucose units, proteins are polymers of amino acids, and nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides.

prompt: Polyethylene can have a molecular weight of up to how many million u?
explanation: Ethylene yields polyethylene, an enormous alkane that may have a molecular weight up to 6 million u and may contain as many as 200,000 monomer units.

prompt: Up to how many ethylene monomer units can a single polyethylene molecule contain?
explanation: Polyethylene may contain as many as 200,000 monomer units and have a molecular weight up to 6 million u.

prompt: Approximately how many million tons of polyethylene are produced worldwide each year?
explanation: Worldwide production of polyethylene is approximately 88 million tons per year.

prompt: Why are polyethylene and other simple alkene polymers called chain-growth polymers?

choices.text: A reactive intermediate adds one monomer after another in a chain reaction
They form when many short polymer chains are joined together end to end
choices.why: An initiator adds to one monomer, and the reactive intermediate then adds monomers one at a time.

choices.text: Their chains are assembled one unit at a time by enzymes, as cellulose is
choices.why: Synthetic chain-growth polymers form with a small amount of an initiator or catalyst, not enzymes.

choices.text: Each monomer releases a small molecule such as water as it adds
choices.why: In chain-growth polymerization the monomers simply add to the growing chain; nothing is lost from each one.

explanation: In chain-growth polymerization, an initiator adds to a C=C bond to give a reactive intermediate. The intermediate reacts with a second monomer to give a new intermediate, which reacts with a third, and so on.

prompt: What role does benzoyl peroxide play in the radical polymerization of ethylene?

choices.text: Heating breaks its weak O–O bond, giving radicals that start the chain
It is the monomer that makes up most of the polymer chain
choices.why: Ethylene is the monomer; benzoyl peroxide is a small amount of initiator.

choices.text: It ends the chain by combining with growing radicals
choices.why: It starts the chain. One way the chain ends is when two growing chains combine.

choices.text: It catalyzes the polymerization on the surface of solid particles
choices.why: It isn't a surface catalyst. Heating it breaks the O–O bond to form radicals.

explanation: Initiation begins when heating a small amount of benzoyl peroxide breaks its weak O–O bond. The benzoyloxy radical loses CO2 to give a phenyl radical, Ph·, which adds to ethylene.

prompt: What does the benzoyloxy radical lose to become a phenyl radical, Ph·?

choices.why: No water is lost. The benzoyloxy radical expels carbon dioxide.
It loses CO2, not O2.
The benzoyloxy radical loses CO2; the phenyl radical then adds to ethylene.

explanation: Heating benzoyl peroxide breaks the O–O bond, giving benzoyloxy radicals. Each loses CO2 to give a phenyl radical, Ph·, which starts the polymerization.

prompt: What are the three steps of radical polymerization of ethylene, in order?

choices.why: The chain must be started (initiated) before it can grow.
Termination ends the chain, so it comes last.
Those are steps of polar acid-catalyzed reactions. Radical polymerization goes by initiation, propagation and termination.

explanation: Like many radical reactions, ethylene polymerization occurs in three steps: initiation (radicals form and add to ethylene), propagation (the carbon radical adds to ethylene again and again), and termination (a reaction consumes the radical).

prompt: When a phenyl radical adds to ethylene in the initiation step, what happens to the two electrons of ethylene's π bond?

choices.text: One pairs with the radical's electron in a new C–C bond; one stays on carbon
Both go into the new C–C bond to phenyl, leaving a carbocation on carbon
choices.why: In radical addition each partner supplies one electron to the new bond; no carbocation forms.

choices.text: Both stay on the far carbon, leaving a carbanion next to the phenyl group
choices.why: One π electron is used in the new bond to the phenyl group.

choices.text: Both leave the molecule along with CO2 from the benzoyloxy radical
choices.why: CO2 is lost earlier, from the benzoyloxy radical. The π electrons stay in the molecule.

explanation: One electron from the ethylene double bond pairs up with the odd electron on the phenyl radical to form a new C–C bond, and the other electron remains on carbon. That carbon radical then propagates the chain.

prompt: What is one way the chain process in ethylene polymerization is terminated?

choices.text: Two growing chains combine: 2 R–CH2CH2· → R–CH2CH2CH2CH2–R
A growing radical adds one more ethylene molecule to its end
choices.why: That is propagation; it makes another radical instead of consuming one.

choices.text: Benzoyl peroxide breaks apart into two benzoyloxy radicals
choices.why: That is initiation.

choices.text: A benzoyloxy radical loses CO2 to form a phenyl radical
choices.why: Loss of CO2 is part of initiation, giving the phenyl radical.

explanation: The chain is eventually ended by a reaction that consumes the radical. One possibility is combination of two growing chains, which pairs their odd electrons in a new C–C bond.

prompt: When vinyl monomers such as propylene or styrene polymerize, where do the substituent groups end up?

choices.text: Regularly spaced on alternating carbon atoms along the chain
On every carbon atom along the whole length of the chain
choices.why: Each monomer contributes a CH2 and a substituted carbon, so substituents fall on every other carbon.

choices.text: Only on the carbons at the two ends of each polymer chain
choices.why: Every monomer carries a substituent, so they occur all along the chain.

choices.text: Randomly on either carbon of each monomer unit in the chain
choices.why: Only the more substituted radical forms, so the pattern is regular: alternating carbons.

explanation: Substituted ethylenes, called vinyl monomers, give polymers with substituent groups regularly spaced on alternating carbon atoms along the chain, as in polypropylene and polystyrene.

prompt: When a radical adds to propylene, H2C=CHCH3, during polymerization, which radical intermediate forms?

choices.text: Only the more highly substituted, secondary radical
Only the less substituted, primary radical, RCH2·
choices.why: The primary radical is not formed. As in electrophilic additions, the more substituted intermediate forms.

choices.text: Equal amounts of primary and secondary radicals
choices.why: Only the secondary radical forms.

choices.text: A tertiary radical, the most substituted kind
choices.why: Propylene's double-bond carbons can give only a primary or a secondary radical.

explanation: Radical addition could take place at either end of the double bond, giving a primary (RCH2·) or secondary (R2CH·) radical. Just as in electrophilic additions, only the more highly substituted, secondary radical is formed.

prompt: Which monomer is used to make Teflon?

choices.why: That gives poly(vinyl chloride), used for insulation, films and pipes.
That gives Orlon and Acrilan fibers.
That gives polystyrene, used for foam and moldings.

explanation: Teflon is made from tetrafluoroethylene, F2C=CF2, and is used for gaskets and nonstick coatings (Figure 8.10.1).

prompt: What are Orlon and Acrilan, the polymers made from acrylonitrile, H2C=CHCN, mainly used for?

choices.why: That is Teflon, from tetrafluoroethylene.
That is poly(vinyl acetate).
That is poly(vinyl chloride).

explanation: Acrylonitrile, H2C=CHCN, gives Orlon and Acrilan, which are used for fibers (Figure 8.10.1).

prompt: Which monomer gives Plexiglas (Lucite)?

choices.why: That gives poly(vinyl acetate), used in paint, adhesives and foams.
That gives Teflon, used for gaskets and nonstick coatings.
That gives Orlon and Acrilan fibers.

explanation: Methyl methacrylate, H2C=C(CH3)CO2CH3, gives Plexiglas and Lucite, used for paint, sheets and moldings (Figure 8.10.1).

prompt: Which repeating unit describes poly(vinyl chloride), made from H2C=CHCl?

choices.text: –CH2–CHCl–, with Cl on every other carbon

choices.why: Each monomer has only one Cl, so the chlorines fall on alternating carbons.

choices.text: –CH2–CH2–, with Cl only at the chain ends
choices.why: Every monomer unit carries a chlorine.
Polymerization turns each C=C into single bonds along the chain.

explanation: Mentally break the C=C bond in each monomer and connect the units with single bonds. Each H2C=CHCl becomes –CH2–CHCl–, so the chain has Cl on alternating carbons (Worked Example 8.10.1).

prompt: A segment of poly(vinyl chloride) chain has 10 carbon atoms in its backbone. How many chlorine atoms does it carry?
explanation: Each H2C=CHCl unit adds two backbone carbons and one chlorine, so a 10-carbon segment contains 5 units and 5 chlorines, on alternating carbons.

prompt: A polymer chain has a methoxy group, –OCH3, on every other carbon. What monomer would you use to prepare it?

choices.why: That would put a methoxy group on every carbon.
Ethylene has no methoxy group; it gives polyethylene.
Chain-growth polymers form from alkenes, and this compound has no C=C bond.

explanation: Working backward, each two-carbon repeating unit, –CH2–CH(OCH3)–, comes from one monomer with a C=C bond: H2C=CHOCH3.

prompt: A polymer chain has a chlorine on every carbon atom. What monomer would you use to prepare it?

choices.why: Vinyl chloride puts Cl on every other carbon, as in PVC.
That puts two Cl on every other carbon, not one on each.
Tetrafluoroethylene gives Teflon, with fluorine, not chlorine.

explanation: Each repeating unit, –CHCl–CHCl–, comes from one monomer with a Cl on each double-bond carbon: ClCH=CHCl.
